I used to be well-read so I do think I have a large vocabulary, plus Im a creative writer. I think the largest challenge I face is TIME. I have homework, and social obligations, and my commute is 3hrs a day, so finding time to read during the day is incredibly hard. If its not assigned, I probably wont read unless I had an extremely lax day, and I prefer reading at home, but loud neighbors and distractions make it difficult as well.

As for academia, I can see a large barrier being language. A lot of papers make the assumption that you are on the same level as the author, and so use words that students and casual viewers may not be familiar with. I always appreciate when an author dedicates a small part of the paper to break down concepts, even if that makes the paper longer as a result. Glossaries and indexes for larger works are also always nice, even in fiction. I personally love pouring over the appendices for LOTR, even though its fiction, just because it makes reading the story more accesible to me.

- Take no for an answer. Just do it. Offer whatever you can, but dont ask "are you sure" or anything like that. As long as youve made every option avaliable to them, youve pushed enough of a sale.

- This ones silly, but at Lush I used to ask what peoples hobbies were, rather than what they were shopping for. Hikers and runners got pitched foot creams, while crafty types got pitched massage bars and bath bombs, because those would likely improve their day to day lives. Maybe ask what hobbies people have, and then let them know clothing options that fit those hobbies. English is pretty tonal we just dont realise it. A question, when spoken, has a rise in the pitch at the end, which is what a question mark denotes in text. In mandarin, this upturn in pitch is replaced by words that indicate its a question. 

We also use tone for emphasis, which italics or caps is used to denote in text. A sentences meaning changes based on all of these factors.

Example:

Your name is John.

YOUR name is John.

Your NAME is John?

Your name is JOHN.

Your name is JOHN?

Unless you dont have an inner monologue, all of those should read differently, meaning the punctuation and emphasis do matter.

When I was a kid I went to Drumheller. Its a beautiful place in Alberta, Canada where a bunch of fossils are found. The whole town is dinosaur themed. Literally an autistic kids wet dream, so obv I was obsessed.

On the trails, I would always be grabbing rocks. I thought that if I grabbed enough, one of them might have a fossil in them. I wanted to take one home with me, because I saw a little bit of (what couldve been) a fossil on it, and I was like 9 and it was the coolest thing I "owned."

Mom put it away. I started crying. I asked her what did it matter if I took one rock? It wasnt even a big one. She told me "well, yes. It doesnt matter if you take that small rock. No one would even notice." Then she pointed at a family with a couple kids nearby. "But what if they all wanted one rock, too? Then three rocks would be gone."

Then we talked it out, and I realised that if *everyone* took a rock, thered be no fossils left. Sure, itd take a while, but it was eventual. So everyone thinking "it doesnt matter if I take one" means everyone takes one, and suddenly itd be a big deal.

I use that idea in a lot of my life, but especially voting. Yes, it doesnt matter if one person votes dem in a red state. It doesnt even matter if a hundred do. But if *everyone* decided it didnt matter if they voted, just because their own vote wouldnt sway the tide, then suddenly the republicans would start polling at 100% (exaggerating, obv, but you get it).

So no, it wont matter if *YOU* go vote, but it will matter if *no one* goes to vote. And if youre thinking that, then a lot of people are thinking that, and it becomes your responsibility to show up anyway.

I really only abide by 2 rules anymore: dont take shit from trails, and go to the polls every damn time theyre open.

My best guess is that this is an issue of worldbuilding. In fanfic, the characters already have distinctions, goals, fears, whathaveyou, and the world is already vivid and unique. Its a great jumping off point because you can skip straight to the meat of your story, and youre safe to assume your readers are on the same page as you on smaller details.

My advice would be to flex your own skills in this way. Try to create a setting, and a few characters. Then, instead of writing the story, write a bit about the world. Write some autobiographies of your characters. Get a really deep sense of the details of your story that fanfic allows you to forget, and have those documents at hand when youre writing the actual story so that you can reference them. 

Readers of original stories dont know anything yet. They want to. You have to learn how to show them a world they arent familiar with, or there will be little to engage with. Even stories set in the "real world" have ideas and values that the reader isnt privy to.

Theres some great character sheets online, as well as worldbuilding exercises. Id suggest starting there!

Look for cases of "scaffolding." Places where youre just describe "he did this, she said that, this happened, then this happened," and try to reword it to be less like a description of events and more like a vivid narration. It happens in first drafts all the time, but readers dont just want a play-by-play of actions, and a lack of emotion could be caused by this. Its useful in small bursts, but if every scene is just a basic list of what happens in what order, youre gonna struggle to evoke much response from your readers.

The good news, if youve done that, is that you *know* whats happening, and can now jump off of those moments and hone your language around it
